Florence, Venice, Milan and dozens more — 14th-century Italy wasn't a country. It was a checkerboard of rival city-states, each flying its own flag.

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ The Holy Roman Empire technically claimed northern Italy, and the Papacy held the center — but real power sat with dozens of independent, walled cities that answered to neither.
2/ Florence, Venice, Milan, Genoa, Pisa and Siena weren't just cities — they were sovereign states with their own armies, currencies, laws, and foreign policy, often at war with each other.
3/ Venice and Genoa fought a series of naval wars over Mediterranean trade routes that stretched across nearly two centuries — city-states as full maritime rivals, not just neighbors.
4/ Most city-states didn't even use their own citizens to fight. They hired condottieri — mercenary captains who led professional armies for whichever city paid best that year.
5/ This fragmentation had an upside: competition between rich, independent cities is a big part of why the Renaissance ignited here first — Florence's bankers, not a king, funded Michelangelo.

6/ Italy wouldn't unify into one state until 1861 — five centuries after this map. For most of its history, 'Italy' was a geographic label, not a country.

Which city-state would you have wanted to live in? Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
